subject: physics
chapter_title: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

concepts.title: Centre of Mass of a Two-Body System
concepts.definition: A collection of particles behaves, as far as its overall motion goes, like one point carrying all the mass -- the centre of mass. For two particles it sits on the line joining them, weighted toward the heavier one, at a position found by averaging the coordinates with masses as weights.
concepts.key_idea: The centre of mass is the mass-weighted average position -- heavier particles pull it closer.

solution_steps.explain: Multiply each particle's position coordinate by its mass.
Dividing the weighted sum by the combined mass places the centre of mass.

concepts.title: Motion of the Centre of Mass
concepts.definition: The centre of mass of an isolated system keeps moving uniformly no matter how the parts flail about, because internal forces cancel in pairs. Its velocity equals the total momentum divided by the total mass, so explosions and internal rearrangements can shift the pieces but never the centre's straight-line path.
concepts.key_idea: Internal forces cannot steer the centre of mass -- only external forces can.

solution_steps.explain: Add m v over every particle to get the system's total momentum.
This quotient is the velocity of the centre of mass, constant while no external force acts.
If a shell explodes in flight, its fragments still trace motions whose mass-weighted average follows the original parabola.

concepts.title: Angular Velocity and Linear Speed
concepts.definition: A rigid body turning about a fixed axis carries every particle through the same angle in the same time -- all share one angular velocity, measured in radians per second. Each particle's linear speed is its radius times that angular velocity, which is why points farther from the axis move faster.
concepts.key_idea: One spin rate for the whole body; each point's linear speed grows with its distance from the axis.

solution_steps.explain: Arc length per second equals radius times radians per second.

concepts.title: Torque: the Turning Effect of Force
concepts.definition: Torque measures how effectively a force turns a body about an axis: it grows with the force and with the perpendicular distance (moment arm) from the axis to the force's line of action. Pushing a door at its edge beats pushing near the hinge because the moment arm is longer.
concepts.key_idea: Same force, longer arm, stronger twist -- torque is force times lever distance.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph106.txt lines 341-430 (section 6.7 torque and angular momentum, moment of force, vector product definition)
question_patterns: find the torque produced by the given force at the given moment arm

solution_steps.explain: Force times the perpendicular distance to the axis gives the torque.

concepts.title: Moment of Inertia and Angular Momentum
concepts.definition: A body's opposition to being spun depends on more than mass -- on how far that mass sits from the axis. This rotational sluggishness is the moment of inertia, and multiplying it by angular velocity gives the angular momentum, the rotational counterpart of linear momentum. When no external torque acts, this angular momentum stays constant.
concepts.key_idea: I omega is the rotational momentum; with zero external torque it cannot change -- spin faster by pulling mass inward.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph106.txt lines 400-560 (section 6.7 angular momentum, 6.10 to 6.12 kinematics and dynamics of rotation, conservation of angular momentum, ice skater example)

solution_steps.explain: Moment of inertia times angular velocity gives the angular momentum.
